title: Browser hardening: permissions, extensions, profiles
body_md:
## Let the browser ask, and answer for one site at a time

A video call needs your microphone for the hour it lasts. A coupon page needs nothing from you, yet it once asked to send notifications, and you clicked Allow to make the pop-up go away. The browser keeps both answers in the same list, and that list is worth a visit.

Websites reach your camera, microphone, location, notifications and downloads through the browser, and its site settings show what each one has been given. Prefer a prompt, or a grant for one named site, to a blanket yes. When a legitimate feature stops working, open that site’s entry and allow only what it needs. Cookies are a separate matter. Clearing them or blocking third-party ones cuts some cross-site tracking, but it can also sign you out or break a login embedded in another page. That is a privacy choice, and it will not tell you whether a page is a scam.

Leave the phishing and malware warnings on. Chrome’s Standard Safe Browsing checks pages against known threats. Enhanced Protection can warn about more unknown sites and risky downloads, and it pays for that by sending Google extra URLs, page samples and extension activity, so weigh the trade before you switch it on. Firefox has deceptive-site warnings and tracking controls too, and HTTPS-only mode will alert you before a connection goes unencrypted. Know what HTTPS does and doesn’t say, though. It means the line to **the displayed domain** is private. It says nothing about who picks up at the other end, and a convincing phishing site can have HTTPS too. A certificate warning is never something to click through on the way to a login box. Reach the service by a route you already know.

## Extensions see what you see

Depending on the grant, an extension can read or change the pages you open, including the ones where you sign in. One installed for a single errand and left with access to every site is a contractor who finished in the spring and still walks in with a pass. Open the extension manager and ask of each entry: do I still use it, who publishes it, does it get updates, does it really need all sites? Chrome can limit many extensions to a click or to specific sites, and an extension installed for one task should not keep universal access afterward. A store listing and high ratings are context, not proof of safety, so read the actual permission prompt and check the publisher. And never install an extension because a caller says it will “fix” your bank page.

Profiles keep work, family and everyday browsing apart, each with its own history, cookies and extensions. That cuts down on logging into the wrong account by accident. It does **not** build the kind of wall an operating system builds, and an unsafe extension in a sensitive profile still sees that profile’s pages. Private or incognito mode mostly changes what your own device remembers: history and cookies. The site, your employer and the network operator can still see you. Keep the browser updated, and protect your accounts with a password manager or passkeys. If a suspicious extension already had broad access, remove it, then check the accounts you used while it was active from a device you trust, and follow the service’s recovery steps if you see signs of compromise.

widget_config.goal: Set your browser so that site permissions and extensions match what you actually use, and know what these settings cannot vouch for.
widget_config.today_action: Run your browser’s built-in safety check, then delete one extension you no longer use. For each one that stays, look at what it can reach: camera, notifications, site data.
widget_config.scope: Chrome and Firefox examples checked on 2026-10-20. Menu names shift with the browser, its version and your organization’s policy. The examples, Toma included, are invented. Privacy controls, phishing warnings and profiles guard against different things.

blocks.title: The extension that “fixes” your bank
blocks.situation: A caller tells Toma that online banking will only work again once a browser extension is installed, one that asks to “read and change all sites.”
blocks.analysis: That permission would show the extension every banking page Toma opens, and the caller’s say-so proves nothing about an outage. Toma ends the call and reaches the bank through a saved official route. If there really is an outage, bank support can explain it without any extension.

blocks.title: The microphone that stays muted
blocks.situation: Ten past nine, and Toma has just opened a meeting from a calendar invite. The site is a familiar one, but the browser has kept its microphone blocked ever since an earlier refusal.
blocks.analysis: Toma checks the meeting address against the calendar entry, allows the microphone for that site while the call lasts, and looks at the grant again afterward. The block was the browser doing its job, and a meeting that wants the microphone is ordinary. None of that proves the invitation itself is genuine.

blocks.title: The family laptop
blocks.setup: An invented household: the family laptop carries an old coupon extension, a meeting site and a banking profile. Nothing here is real.

steps.prompt: The coupon extension can read every site, and nobody has opened it in months.

choices.text: Remove it once you have confirmed nobody still needs it.
choices.consequence: The access nobody was using is gone.
choices.explanation: Wide access has to keep earning its place. A purpose it once had is no reason to leave it running.

choices.text: Keep it. It came from the official store and might come in handy.
choices.consequence: It keeps its view of every page you open.
choices.explanation: A store listing says where it came from, not why it still needs every site.

steps.prompt: A meeting site asks for the microphone just as a scheduled call begins.

choices.text: Allow the microphone for every site, for good.
choices.consequence: Sites that have no use for it can now reach for the microphone too.
choices.explanation: One meeting is no reason to hand every site a standing yes.

choices.text: Check the meeting address, allow the site for this call, then review the grant afterward.
choices.consequence: The call works without a global microphone grant.
choices.explanation: Attach the permission to one verified site and one purpose.

steps.prompt: Chrome offers Enhanced Protection. What should guide your choice?

choices.text: Weigh the stronger warnings against the extra data sent to Google.
choices.consequence: You choose knowingly, and at least Standard protection stays on.
choices.explanation: Enhanced is a privacy trade, not a requirement.

choices.text: Switch off every warning, for the sake of privacy.
choices.consequence: You lose a useful signal about threats.
choices.explanation: You do not have to pick an extreme: Standard protection sits between the two.

steps.prompt: A page imitating your bank shows a padlock, or your browser’s “secure” icon, by the address.

choices.text: Sign in. The connection is encrypted.
choices.consequence: Your password goes straight to whoever runs the lookalike.
choices.explanation: Encryption cannot correct a wrong destination.

choices.text: Close it and open the bank through its saved app or a bookmark.
choices.consequence: You never type your credentials at the wrong domain.
choices.explanation: HTTPS protects the trip to that domain, not the honesty of whoever runs it.

blocks.debrief: Play it again and, for each choice, name the boundary the control actually guards: a site’s permission, an extension’s reach into your pages, the warning service, or the road to a domain, which is all HTTPS covers.

blocks.title: Carry it to the next browser

questions.prompt: You need an extension on one site only. Which grant fits best?

choices.text: On click, or limited to that one site, where the browser allows it.
choices.explanation: Pages unrelated to the task stay out of its reach.
That is far wider than the job.

questions.prompt: Since you began blocking cookies, a genuine sign-in widget has stopped working. What next?

choices.text: Turn off all browser protection everywhere.
choices.explanation: One site’s trouble does not justify sweeping changes.

choices.text: Open that site’s settings and allow the narrow exception it needs.
choices.explanation: Privacy controls can break legitimate embedded logins.

questions.prompt: What does the HTTPS on a shopping page actually establish?

choices.text: The connection to the domain shown in the address bar is encrypted.
choices.explanation: A scammer can get HTTPS for a lookalike domain as well.
Encryption says nothing about whether the merchant is honest.

questions.prompt: Does a separate browser profile contain malware the way a separate OS would?

choices.text: Yes. A risky extension turns harmless there.
choices.explanation: An extension can still act on the pages inside its own profile.

choices.text: No. It mainly separates browser state and extensions.
choices.explanation: Profiles help with mixing up accounts, but they are not a sandbox for the device.
